title: Indian Diaspora Is Building a 20,000-Square-Foot Museum in Washington to Tell India's 11,000-Year Story.
excerpt: The India Heritage Center, led by Atlanta-based Dr. Amitabh Sharma, will use VR, immersive galleries, and a 350-seat auditorium to present a civilisational narrative no American museum has attempted before.
body:
After nearly eight years of research and planning, the Indian American community is preparing to build something the United States has never had: a permanent museum in Washington, D.C., dedicated entirely to India's civilisational story.

The India Heritage Center, as the project is called, is being led by Dr. Amitabh Sharma, an Atlanta-based educationist and community leader who has spent years arguing that India's contributions to science, philosophy, culture, and governance have never been presented in the depth they deserve — at least not in the West, and certainly not in the American capital.

"Indian history and Indian civilisation has never been portrayed in the strength that it deserves," Sharma told IANS. "It is important in today's perspective, more importantly, to be able to tell the world that this is the rich civilisation, rich heritage that we have."

## A 20,000-Square-Foot Complex

The proposed museum would be a 20,000-square-foot complex housing ten galleries, a 350-seat auditorium, a library, reception facilities, and a gift centre. The design centres on immersive technology — virtual reality, augmented reality, interactive audio-video systems, murals, and physical artefacts — to walk visitors through more than 11,000 years of Indian history.

The galleries would span from the Indus Valley civilisation and Vedic traditions through the Mughal and colonial periods to India's emergence as a modern democratic nation. Scientific contributions, spiritual traditions, literary heritage, and the story of the global Indian diaspora would each have dedicated space.

## Why Washington

Sharma and his team chose Washington deliberately. The city is home to the Smithsonian Institution, the National Museum of African American History and Culture, the Holocaust Memorial Museum, and dozens of other institutions that tell the stories of communities and civilisations. India, despite having a diaspora of over 4.4 million in the United States alone, has no equivalent presence on the National Mall or anywhere else in the capital.

"So I think it is time that we told our story," Sharma said. "Telling our story in a very compelling narrative."

The project also aims to reach beyond the Indian community. Sharma emphasised the importance of sensitising mainstream Americans and other communities to India's diverse traditions — particularly its history of coexistence and its tradition of providing refuge to persecuted communities across millennia.

## The Diaspora Angle

For the 4.4 million Indian Americans in the United States, the museum would serve a dual purpose: a cultural anchor for younger generations growing up far from India, and a public statement that India's story belongs alongside those already being told in Washington's museum district.

The Indian American community is already among the most educated and highest-earning immigrant groups in the country. But cultural representation in public institutions has lagged behind economic and professional success. The India Heritage Center is designed to close that gap.

The project is still in the fundraising and site-selection phase. Organisers have not disclosed a target budget, but comparable museum projects in Washington have cost between $300 million and $500 million. The team plans to launch a formal campaign in the coming months, with Sharma describing the timeline as "ambitious but achievable."

*Sources: IANS, Indian.community*
